# RQ2 - Immune-related signatures

Are 18-gene T-cell–inflamed GEP (see D6; Ayers et al. (2017)) **associated** (NOT RESPONSE + RESPONSE PREDICTION) with treatment response?

Reference: 10.1172/JCI91190

-   Using dataset as is (not filtered etc)

**Suggested tasks:**

-   **Q2.1:** Identify the 18 genes included in the published T-cell–inflamed GEP (gene expression profile) and examine their expression in the dataset.

-   **Q2.2:** Calculate a T-cell–inflamed GEP score for each patient.

-   **Q2.3**: Investigate whether patients with higher GEP scores are more likely to respond to anti-PD-L1 treatment.

-   **Q2.4:** Interpret the biological significance of your findings and discuss why a high T- cell–inflamed GEP score does not necessarily guarantee treatment response.

## Q1: Identify the 18 genes included in the published T-cell–inflamed GEP (gene expression profile) and examine their expression in the dataset.

```{r}
# STEP 1: create panel
GEPs <- c("TIGIT", "CD27", "CD8A", "PDCD1LG2", "LAG3", "CD274", "CXCR6", "CMKLR1", "NKG7", "CCL5", "PSMB10", "IDO1", "CXCL9", "HLA-DQA1", "CD276", "STAT1", "HLA-DRB1", "HLA-E")

# checking we have 18 genes
length(GEPs)

# assessing dataset genes
all_genes <- rownames(tpm)
length(all_genes)

# checking gene name format
head(all_genes)



# STEP 2: Align tpm to clinical table
clinical <- clinical[clinical$BOR %in% c("NR", "R"), ]
tpm <-  tpm[, clinical$sample_id]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(tpm), as.character(clinical$sample_id)))
    

      
# STEP 3: Checking GEPs are present in dataset
GEPs %in% rownames(tpm)
GEPs[GEPs %in% rownames(tpm)]



# STEP 4: Extract + logtransform g.expression
# IMPORTANT TO LOG TRANSFORM (visualization + scoring)
GEP_expression <- log2(tpm[GEPs, , drop = FALSE] +1)
dim(GEP_expression) # 192 patients



#STEP 5: Checking expression
# per gene
summary(t(GEP_expression))

# median expression per gene
apply(GEP_expression, 1, median)

# checking low counts (how many patients have an expression value = 0, per gene)
rowSums(GEP_expression == 0)
```

Most genes are expressed in most patients, except HLA-DQA1 (absent in 129 patients!)

```{r}
# STEP 6: Visualize
annotation <- data.frame(Response = clinical$BOR,
                         row.names = clinical$sample_id)

ord <- order(clinical$BOR)

pheatmap(GEP_expression[, ord],
         #standardize each gene ACROSS patients
         scale = "row",      
         annotation_col = annotation[ord, , drop = FALSE],
         cluster_cols = FALSE,
         show_colnames = FALSE)

#checking correlation of genes
pheatmap(cor(t(GEP_expression)))
```

heatmap: suggest patterns –\> confirm using wilcoxon test

-   standardized expression for each gene + patient

-   some concentration of higher expression in responder group

-   row = genes, cols = patients

-   left tree = hierchal clustering (based on genes with sim patterns)

## **Q2.2:** Calculate a T-cell–inflamed GEP score for each patient.

-   Standardize each gene across patients (avoid dominating genes)

-   average across the 18 genes per patient (1 nr per patient –\> if high =\> more inflammed compared to other patients)

-   day 6

```{r}
# STEP 1: confirming data
dim(GEP_expression)

stopifnot(identical(colnames(GEP_expression),
                    as.character(clinical$sample_id)))

# STEP 2: Check no gene is constant (0 var cant be standardized)
gene_sd <- apply(GEP_expression, 1, sd)
gene_sd
any(gene_sd == 0)


```

No constant genes –\> continue to standardization

scale = standardize cols (have to transpose t(), as genes are rows)

transpose gene expression –\> scale –\> transpose back again (genes = rows)

```{r}
# STEP 3: Standardize across patients
GEP_scaled <- t(scale(t(GEP_expression)))

# checking standarzation 
round(rowMeans(GEP_scaled), 10) #mean of 0
apply(GEP_scaled, 1, sd) #sd of 1

# STEP 4: Average ACROSS genes
GEP_scores <- colMeans(GEP_scaled)

length(GEP_scores)
summary(GEP_scores)
head(GEP_scores)


# STEP 5: add clinical data (building data frame)
df <- data.frame(
  sample_id = clinical$sample_id,
  BOR = factor(clinical$BOR, levels = c("NR", "R")),
  GEP_score = GEP_scores
)

#safety check --> confirm scores matches correct patients
stopifnot(identical(df$sample_id, names(GEP_scores)))
head(df)
table(df$BOR, useNA = "ifany") #add NA column if any present


# STEP 6: visualize
hist(df$GEP_score, breaks = 20, main = "GEP_score distribution")
tapply(df$GEP_score, df$BOR, median)
```

colMeans = average down each col (patients across 18 genes) –\> output = vector with l = 192

NR = 167

R = 25

## **Q2.3**: Investigate whether patients with higher GEP scores are more likely to respond to anti-PD-L1 treatment.

= Compare GEP score to response group

Our df is defined with NR as reference group

Step 1 = overview of medians + quartiles (size + direction of difference) of NR + R groups

Wilcon rank sum test = compare 2 independent groups (without assuming normal distr.) (rec week6)

-   0 hyp: scores in the 2 groups come from the same distribution

```{r}
# reusing df from 2.3

# STEP 1: Describe each group (extra)
tapply(df$GEP_score, df$BOR, summary)



# STEP 2: Test difference between NR and R (wilcoxon rank sum test)
GEP_test <- wilcox.test(GEP_score ~ BOR, data = df, exact = FALSE)

# STEP 3: Plot difference
ggplot(df,
       aes(x= BOR, y = GEP_score)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) + #dont draw outliers twice
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.6) + #add small hori shift to each point
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = Inf,
           label = paste0("p = ", signif(GEP_test$p.value, 3)),
           hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.5) + 
  labs(x = "Response (NR = progressive disease, R = complete response)",
       y = "T cell inflamed GEP score") + 
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# advanced plot

# Descriptive group labels with patient counts (extra)
n_per_group <- table(df$BOR)
group_labels <- c(
  NR = paste0("Progressive disease (NR)\nn = ", n_per_group["NR"]),
  R  = paste0("Complete response (R)\nn = ", n_per_group["R"])
)

group_colours <- c(NR = "#D9534F", R = "#2E86C1")   # red = NR, blue = R

ggplot(df, aes(x = BOR, y = GEP_score, fill = BOR, colour = BOR)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.25, width = 0.5) +   # don't draw outliers twice
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = Inf,
           label = paste0("Wilcoxon p = ", signif(GEP_test$p.value, 3)),
           hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.5, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colours) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_colours) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = group_labels) +
  labs(
    title = "T-cell–inflamed GEP score by treatment response",
    subtitle = "Each dot is one patient; dashed line = cohort average (score 0)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "T-cell–inflamed GEP score\n(mean z-score of 18 genes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Plot: Each dot = patient sample, height = patient T cell inflamed GEP score

-   Median of responders are higher than NR =\> responders tend to have higher GEP scores

-   OBS R is smaller than NR (group size)

Adding quantifying step on top of p value estimate (not sure if i should include)

```{r}
# Prob that a random R patient will have a higher score than a random NR patient
n_NR <- sum(df$BOR == "NR"); n_R <-  sum(df$BOR == "R")

AUC <- 1 - unname(GEP_test$statistic) / (n_NR * n_R)
AUC #if 1 = perfect, if 0.5 = no seperation


# Odds of response per 1 SD increase in score
df$GEP_SD <-  as.numeric(scale(df$GEP_score))
fit <- glm((BOR == "R") ~ GEP_SD, data = df, family = binomial)
exp(cbind(OR = coef(fit), confint.default(fit)))["GEP_SD", ]
summary(fit)
```

AUC = 0.74 =\> some seperation of groups (prob that a random responser has a higher GEP score than a random non responder)

-   AUC = effect size (no validated perf eval, no held out data)

Each 1 SD increase in score –\> \* odds of complete response by 2.4

ODDS ARE NOT PROBS! (odds = p/(1-p))

High inflammed profile scores are associated with higher odds of complete response in our data

"Each one-standard-deviation increase in the T-cell–inflamed score was associated with 2.4-fold higher odds of complete response (OR 2.41, 95% CI 1.50–3.87). The wide interval reflects uncertainty in the effect size, and this is an association within one cohort, not a validated predictor."

## **Q2.4:** Interpret the biological significance of your findings and discuss why a high T- cell–inflamed GEP score does not necessarily guarantee treatment response.

-   Have analyzed patterns in our dataset

    -   Logistic regression: does score + response move together in the data?

    -   odds ratio of

-   In this cohort

-   Associated with (score NOT = response (havent adjusted for confounders eg tumor purity (Q4))

-   Higher odds (not prob)

-   CANNOT conclude higher t cell inflammed GEP scores = predicts individual patient response!

    -   Same data used to find + test pattern

    -   No threshold + no validation (no cut off score for when someone is a likely responder)

Conclusions:

-   Responders have a higher T-cell–inflamed GEP score on average

-   Higher score –\> higher odds of response

Cannot conclude:

-   Score value indicates response

-   Score dictates which patient will respond to treatment

-   If the score would be similar in another cohort

Higher T cell inflammes score = tumor has already activated the interferon gamma driven T cell response (required for checkpoint blockade to work)

The genes are indicative of an inflammed tumour microenvironment.\
The 18 genes are interferon-gamma marker genes (CD8A, NKG7, CCL5, CXCL9 (chemokine, recruits activated CD8+ effector T cells)), STAT1) and checkpoint or antigen presenting genes (CD274, PDCD1LG2, LAG3, TIGIT, HLA-DRB1, PSMB10)

Chemokine recruits activated CD8+ effector T cells –\> T cells release IFN-gamma –\> raises antigen presentation + checkpoint ligand expression

-   High score = pre existing anti tumor immune response –\> amplified (breaks on this removed) in PD1 therapy

Why high score IS NOT = guaranteed response:

-   The score is 1 dim = measures how MUCH immune response, not if it works

-   T cells can be present but not within the tumor microenv. (stuck in stroma around tumor)

    -   BULK RNA averages all tissues (includes stroma cells etc)

-   Other cells can cancel T cell activation (eg neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages)

-   Tumor cells can be masked from T cells

-   Consider tumour mutational burden + neoantigens
